item.content:encoded:
Gov.-elect Tony Ada and Lt. Gov.-elect E.J. Calvo said their incoming administration will open cabinet and senior staff positions to public applicants, with an emphasis on professional experience, qualifications, and commitment to public service rather than political affiliation.

During their first press conference as governor and lieutenant governor-elect, the two outlined plans to establish an online application portal where interested residents, including current government employees, can submit resumes and apply for positions within the incoming administration.

Jadeen Perez, who will chair the transition team’s Committee on Administration and Appointees, said the committee plans to begin accepting applications after the election results are certified on Nov. 19.

Applicants will undergo background checks and an evaluation of their qualifications before the committee submits recommendations to Ada and Calvo.

Ada said the application process will be open to anyone interested in serving, including members of the current administration.

“The bottom line is, everybody working together, regardless of party affiliation,” Ada said. “Election is over. Now it’s time for everybody to come together and work together.”

The incoming administration has also established three principal transition committees to guide the transfer of government responsibilities. The Committee on Government Operations and Efficiency, chaired by Nate Denight, will review the operations of government agencies, identify opportunities to improve efficiency, and assess existing challenges. The Committee on Administration and Appointees will oversee the recruitment and evaluation of potential cabinet members and senior staff, while the Committee on Inaugural Arrangements, chaired by Piti Mayor Jesse Alig, will coordinate inauguration preparations.

Denight said the government operations committee will establish additional subcommittees to review the island’s 52 government agencies. The committees will meet with agency management and staff to identify what is working, what needs improvement, and what resources may be needed.

Their findings will be compiled into a final transition report outlining each department’s current situation, objectives, and recommendations. Transition chair Jerry Crisostomo said the report will help Ada and Calvo determine their administration’s priorities and guide appointments ahead of their expected Jan. 4 start in office.

Ada said the incoming administration will first focus on completing a smooth transition and assessing the government’s financial position and operational needs before determining its immediate priorities.

One policy direction the incoming administration has already identified is a dedicated executive leadership position for tourism and destination development, separate from economic development. Calvo said they may be the first administration ever to dedicate an executive position to the industry of tourism.

“The position we’re looking at is actually tourism and destination development, separate from economic development, which is important,” Calvo said, “I think that would probably have fallen under economic development in the past, but we need to look at diversifying our economy and also protecting other growing industries separately.”

Ada said the position would reflect tourism’s significant impact on Guam’s economy and employment, particularly as the island’s tourism industry continues to face challenges.

When asked about their first 100 days in office, Ada said the administration will begin implementing its campaign plans after evaluating the government’s needs and establishing its leadership team. Calvo identified tourism, economic development, federal relations, and education as among the areas that will require attention.

When asked what the new administration is most excited to begin working on as they work toward a smooth government transition, they said they plan to continue monthly community cleanups, which began during the campaign.

“We want to still get out there and keep our community clean,” Ada said. “We want to ensure that, as we continue to move along within the first 100 days of our administration, that we start implementing our plans and get it to what we said during our campaign. You’re going to start seeing the implementation of those plans come to fruition.”

Ada and Calvo said they will seek guidance from former Republican governors and lieutenant governors to assist with the transition. Those invited to serve as honorary transition advisers include former governors Felix Camacho and Eddie Calvo, along with former lieutenant governors Ray Tenorio, Mike Cruz and Kaleo Moylan.

The transition team says additional appointments and opportunities for public participation will be announced in the coming weeks. Updates are expected through the incoming administration’s website and social media platforms.

item.content:encoded:
The Commonwealth Election Commission is expected to certify the results of the 2026 general election Friday, formally triggering a 14-day countdown to runoff elections on Nov. 20 for governor and attorney general, according to CEC Executive Director Kayla Igitol Magofna.

Magofna said Thursday that election commissioners are scheduled to certify the official results, setting into motion preparations for the runoff election required under CNMI law when no candidate secures more than 50% of all votes cast and counted.

"So we have to have an election 14 days after," Magofna said.

The certification will finalize results from the Nov. 3 general election and establish the timeline for distributing runoff ballots and preparing polling sites across the Commonwealth.

According to the CEC, absentee voters who requested ballots for the general election will automatically receive absentee ballots for the runoff election. Election officials said no new requests for overseas absentee ballots will be accepted, although over-the-counter absentee voting will remain available.

Earlier, the commission mailed out 1,420 absentee ballots for the general election. Election officials counted 886 absentee ballots in the final tabulation and noted that ballots had to be received on Saipan on or before Election Day to be included in the certified results.

For the runoff election, the commission said it will continue to receive absentee ballots for up to 14 days after Election Day pursuant to its established procedures.

The certified results are expected to confirm runoff contests in both the governor's and attorney general's races.

In the gubernatorial contest, the Republican ticket of Ralph DLG Torres and Benjamin Jones Jr. led the field with 6,437 votes, or 49.5% of ballots cast, narrowly missing the majority needed to avoid a runoff. The independent ticket of Blas Jonathan Attao and Edmund Villagomez finished second with 5,043 votes, or 38.7%, advancing to the Nov. 20 runoff.

The independent team of Lawrence F. Camacho and Edith Deleon Guerrero placed third with 1,537 votes, or 11.8%.

The attorney general race also failed to produce a majority winner. Attorney Joaquin DLG Torres received 5,073 votes, or 39.7%, while attorney Michael Evangelista secured 3,854 votes, or 30.2%. Attorney Jonathan Robert Glass Jr. followed closely with 3,836 votes, or 30.1%.

Under CNMI law, the top two vote-getters advance to a runoff when no gubernatorial candidate or attorney general candidate receives more than half of all votes cast and counted.

The Commonwealth had 18,521 registered voters for the 2026 election. More than 13,000 voters cast ballots in the gubernatorial race, leaving roughly 5,500 registered voters who did not participate.

Election officials said registered voters who did not vote in the general election remain eligible to cast ballots in the Nov. 20 runoff election.

With certification anticipated Friday, election administrators will have two weeks to complete preparations for what is expected to be a closely watched runoff that will determine the Commonwealth's next governor and attorney general.

item.content:encoded:
The 39 th Guam Legislature will bring new faces, as well as some returning senators, into Guam’s lawmaking body.

A number of senators in the 38 th Guam Legislature gave up their seats to run for higher office. Republican Speaker Frank Blas Jr., Republican Vice Speaker Tony Ada and Democratic Sens. Therese Terlaje and Joe San Agustin all ran for governor, with Ada winning the island’s highest office.

Democratic Sens. Sabina Perez and Tina Muna Barnes ran for lieutenant governor.

That left nine incumbents, all of whom won reelection.

They are Republicans Sabrina Salas Matanane, Jesse Lujan, Chris Duenas, Shelly Calvo, Telo Taitague, Vincent Borja and Eulogio Shawn Gumatatao. Democratic incumbents reelected were Chris Barnett and William Parkinson.

Former Democratic Sens. Amanda Shelton, Telena Nelson and Clynton Ridgell were elected Tuesday, along with Democratic legislative newcomers Donna Quinata and Kallen Perez.

Hoa Nyugen is the Republican newcomer, giving the party an 8-7 majority in the 39 th Legislature.

item.title: 'All Things Considered' bids farewell to host Mary Louise Kelly
item.description: From NPR News, this is ALL THINGS CONSIDERED. I'm Ailsa Chang. And I'm Juana Summers. It has been 26 years since NPR listeners first heard this voice bringing them the news.
item.content:encoded:
From NPR News, this is ALL THINGS CONSIDERED. I'm Ailsa Chang.

And I'm Juana Summers. It has been 26 years since NPR listeners first heard this voice bringing them the news.

David Shayler was arrested the moment he stepped onto British soil.

SUMMERS: Wow. OK, you might not recognize the voice, but you definitely know the reporter.

KELLY: For NPR News, this is Mary Louise Kelly in London.

CHANG: That's right. That is our co-host, Mary Louise, and we are bidding her, today, farewell. She's stepping away from ALL THINGS CONSIDERED, but do not worry because she's still going to be contributing to NPR's airwaves. We just wanted to take some time today to say goodbye and to celebrate her tremendous run in the host chair.

DETROW: Her journey with ALL THINGS CONSIDERED began in 2001 when she walked into the office of longtime host Robert Siegel for an interview to become the editor of ALL THINGS CONSIDERED.

ROBERT SIEGEL, BYLINE: And I was so impressed with her that when she walked out of my office, I called the executive producer before she got there and said, you hire this woman. Just hire her. She's terrific.

DETROW: They did hire her. Mary Louise edited the show for three years before transitioning back to reporting. She launched NPR's intelligence beat.

SUMMERS: One of her editors, Bruce Auster, says her determination and precision stood out, as did her approach to journalism.

BRUCE AUSTER, BYLINE: Mary Louise believed that her role is essentially to sort of bear witness, to be able to go places and see what the audience needs to know.

SUMMERS: Take her trip around Afghanistan with then-Defense Secretary Robert Gates.

AUSTER: The challenge is, is that you're in the bubble, you're trapped, and you can only see what you can see. But you're also constrained in terms of your ability to file because you're spending half the day on a helicopter.

SUMMERS: They had to have a story ready that same day for ALL THINGS CONSIDERED.

AUSTER: So the piece essentially becomes Mary Louise on a helicopter, sound of helicopter, getting off helicopter, describing what she sees on the ground...

KELLY: Marines are swarming the roofs of the mud huts around us, machine guns in hand.

AUSTER: ...Getting back on helicopter...

KELLY: All right, we got the all clear, so they're just loading us up in...

KELLY: We are off to Kabul and another round of meetings to plan the way forward in this war.

AUSTER: It captured the moment. It bore witness to what was happening, and it told the story in an entertaining way.

CHANG: Well, Mary Louise brought that same ethos to her job as a host. She's taken listeners to the offices of independent election monitors in Russia...

KELLY: Oh, my God, they've just opened the ballot box.

ROMAN UDOT: They took it from under their clothes. They stuff it, stuff it, stuff it.

CHANG: ...To a military parade in North Korea...

KELLY: Kim Jong Un has just arrived in the square.

UNIDENTIFIED PERSON: We are happy that we can stand, and we can punch the America.

CHANG: For Mary Louise, building an understanding of the world is also about asking questions of those in power, even the people in charge at NPR.

DETROW: In 2017, amid a newsroom sexual harassment scandal, Mary Louise interviewed then-CEO Jarl Mohn. She was guest hosting at the time, not yet a permanent host of the show, which made what happened next even more remarkable.

SIEGEL: This is someone with whom you have a professional relationship, the boss of your boss' boss, someone whose opinion of you might count for a lot in your future. And also people will be listening, and they'll be thinking, is this host going really easy on this guy because he's her boss?

RENITA JABLONSKI: I remember Mary Louise was the same as she is every single day, calm and focused.

item.title: The economy propelled Democrats to victory. What can they actually do about it?
item.description: After big wins in midterm elections, Democrats say they are clear-eyed about their mandate come January. HAKEEM JEFFRIES: We're going to fight to make sure that we make this country affordable for every single American.
item.content:encoded:
After big wins in midterm elections, Democrats say they are clear-eyed about their mandate come January.

HAKEEM JEFFRIES: We're going to fight to make sure that we make this country affordable for every single American.

KELLY: That's Hakeem Jeffries, the presumptive next speaker of the House. Now, again, Democrats won control of both houses of Congress this week, but they will face Republican roadblocks in the Senate plus the threat of presidential vetoes. So how much can they actually do to deliver on their campaign promises? NPR congressional correspondent Barbara Sprunt is here to take that question. Hey, Barbara.

KELLY: OK, so Democrats won big, really big, but not big enough to override a veto from the president. Is there a risk that voters will be disappointed by what Democrats can actually achieve on, say, cost of living and affordability?

SPRUNT: Well, there is a risk. But I think it comes down to communication. You know, I've talked to Democrats who say they need to make sure that they don't overpromise and underdeliver and that they have to be upfront about their own limitations here. I was talking to Matt Bennett about this. He's the co-founder of Third Way, a centrist Democratic think tank.

MATT BENNETT: What Democrats were really promising was, return us to power. We will put a check on Trump for two years and then when we get to the White House in 2028, we can actually make your lives better. And it isn't clear to me that voters heard the entire message. They might have just heard the last part. And so there could be some real disappointment.

SPRUNT: But this is a needle to thread, you know, because Democrats want to show that they're taking action, that they're not just waiting around for two years.

KELLY: That they don't want to wait around - I got it. But have they laid out any detail about how they're going to get around Republican roadblocks?

SPRUNT: Well, Democrats control the agenda, which means they get to decide what they bring up for a vote. And people may recall, last year, there was an effort to release the Epstein files. Republican leadership tried to prevent it from getting to the floor. But after some maneuvering, it did get to the floor, and Republicans voted nearly unanimously alongside Democrats to release the files. So Democrats will be in a position to force Republicans to go on the record, often on measures that have a lot of public support. And there also could be areas for real bipartisanship, I think. You know, this has happened before. I think back to 2007, after Democrats won control of Congress. They passed a minimum wage increase, and it was a Republican president, George Bush, who signed it into law.

KELLY: Yeah. Barbara, let me ask about one area where - speaking of bipartisanship - there seems to be bipartisan agreement among voters. The gas prices are too high. Can a Democratic-controlled Congress do much about that?

SPRUNT: This is a tough one for lawmakers because they don't have a direct path towards lowering fuel prices beyond trying to end the war in Iran. And they can try to do that in a few ways. They can try to force Trump's hand with a war powers resolution. You know, historically, presidents of both parties have largely ignored those. An alternative would be using must-pass legislation like funding for the government and appropriations bill and adding a provision to explicitly stop funds from being used in the war. That, of course, could be vetoed by the president.

KELLY: Right. That's the nub of this - right? - that whatever they do, whatever they send his way, the president's going to have his veto pen ready.

SPRUNT: That's right. I mean, but he is a wild card. You know, he has said that he will veto everything. He's also said that he could see himself cutting deals with Democrats. So Democrats say, despite all of the mixed signals that he's sending, it's important to send the bills to his desk. Here's New York Democratic Senator Kirsten Gillibrand on Morning Edition yesterday.

KIRSTEN GILLIBRAND: If we have a bill that is bipartisan to restore health care for the people who lost their Medicaid or to improve access to affordable medicines and other things, like, I dare him to veto that. I dare him to stand in front of the American people and say, you don't deserve access to healthcare.

KELLY: She's saying this is a tool in their toolbox.

SPRUNT: This is a tool, and they plan to use it. If the president vetoes legislation that's popular with the public, it's news cycle after news cycle of Trump vetoes bill to lower healthcare costs, or what have you. You know, it places the blame for stuff not getting done squarely on his shoulders.

KELLY: NPR's Barbara Sprunt. Transcript provided by NPR, Copyright NPR.

item.description: At the top of the charts this week is a band that has waited a long time for its first No. 1 album. Stephen Thompson of NPR Music explains. STEPHEN THOMPSON, BYLINE: This week's Billboard pop charts reflect the seven days just before Halloween, so a few spooky perennials haunt the latest charts. Scan the new Hot 100, and you'll find Michael Jackson's "Thriller," Rockwell's "Somebody's Watching Me,
item.content:encoded:
At the top of the charts this week is a band that has waited a long time for its first No. 1 album. Stephen Thompson of NPR Music explains.

STEPHEN THOMPSON, BYLINE: This week's Billboard pop charts reflect the seven days just before Halloween, so a few spooky perennials haunt the latest charts. Scan the new Hot 100, and you'll find Michael Jackson's "Thriller," Rockwell's "Somebody's Watching Me," and a signature song from "The Nightmare Before Christmas," "This Is Halloween."

(SOUNDBITE OF SONG, "THIS IS HALLOWEEN")

UNIDENTIFIED ACTORS: (As characters, singing) This is Halloween. This is Halloween. Halloween, Halloween, Halloween, Halloween.

THOMPSON: The week's biggest surprise is a milestone performance for a long-running band that knows its way around the darkness. For the first time in a career spanning 25 years, the Gothic pop punk band My Chemical Romance has the No. 1 album in the country.

(SOUNDBITE OF SONG, "WELCOME TO THE BLACK PARADE")

MY CHEMICAL ROMANCE: (Singing) Because one day, I'll leave you a phantom to lead you in the summer to join the black parade.

THOMPSON: "The Black Parade" came out in 2006, when it debuted and peaked at No. 2 on the Billboard albums chart. The record remained My Chemical Romance's highest-charting album in the 20 years following its original release. And in honor of "The Black Parade's" 20th anniversary, the band has gone all out to commemorate the album.

(SOUNDBITE OF SONG, "WELCOME TO THE BLACK PARADE")

MY CHEMICAL ROMANCE: (Singing) Your memory will carry on, will carry on.

THOMPSON: My Chemical Romance has been playing songs from "The Black Parade" on tour for months now, and it's just released a deluxe edition of the album with bonus tracks. That reissue includes many different versions on vinyl and CD, which has helped give "The Black Parade" a huge sales boost. "The Black Parade" has now set a new Billboard chart record. The 20-year gap between its debut and its first week at No. 1 has been the longest in chart history. Stephen Thompson, NPR Music.

(SOUNDBITE OF MY CHEMICAL ROMANCE SONG, "WELCOME TO THE BLACK PARADE") Transcript provided by NPR, Copyright NPR.

item.content:encoded:
The blue tsunami of Democratic victories in the midterms was partly powered by a groundswell of support among Black voters. That's especially true in the South, where many voting rights activists had feared the Supreme Court decision gutting the Voting Rights Act would have weakened Black voting power. To help us make sense of all of this, we have called Andra Gillespie. She's a professor of political science at Emory University in Atlanta. Welcome.

CHANG: So I know we're just a few days out from the election, and there are still some races that have yet to be called, but overall, how big of an increase in Black voter participation did we see in this election compared to the 2024 election or even previous midterm election cycles, do you think?

GILLESPIE: So I'm going to use my state of Georgia as an example because Georgia does collect data on voter turnout by race. That would be really helpful in this election cycle. So in absolute terms, compared to 2022, we saw higher voter turnout amongst African Americans, Latinos and Asian American voters in the state of Georgia. White voters actually had lower voter turnout compared to 2022. And so that actually helps to contribute to overall Black and Asian American voters in particular making up a larger share of the 2026 electorate than they did amongst registered voters.

CHANG: What about Black male voters? I want to focus on them for a moment because President Trump did make some inroads with Black men back in 2024, even though they still largely voted for Kamala Harris. And now I see that exit polls are showing a swing back to Democrats among Black men. So I'm curious, why do you think this is happening, or what is happening?

GILLESPIE: If I had to proffer a hypothesis...

GILLESPIE: ...It's probably because of economic issues. One of the things that's actually really interesting nationally if we look at the voter poll or the exit poll data, the economy ranked as the top issue amongst voters overall, but especially in southern states like South Carolina and Georgia and Mississippi, Black voters were actually more likely to cite the economy as their top issue than we saw in those national averages.

CHANG: I want to talk about the historic nature of this election that maybe transcends party politics. I mean, in the governor races, you see this especially. There were a number of historic firsts. You had David Crowley elected as Wisconsin's first Black governor, Keisha Lance Bottoms, the country's first Black woman governor, Byron Donalds, who was elected to become Florida's first Black governor. And I know that these are all different races. These are distinct individuals I'm talking about. But do you see any through line in the role that Black voters may have played in these particular historic wins?

GILLESPIE: Well, yes, but I think there's also this larger issue of candidates supply and Black politicians feeling confident enough that they can run for statewide office. You know, a generation ago, two generations ago, this would have been a risky move, so if you had a really safe congressional seat, like Congressman Donalds', had you might not choose to run (ph), especially if you were a Democrat for statewide office, because you're going to give up a guaranteed seat in order to take a risk and run for a seat that you might not eventually win.

GILLESPIE: Well, there's been more examples of Blacks being able to run successfully for statewide office in both the Democratic and the Republican Parties. And I think Stacey Abrams' work in 2018, though it was unsuccessful in getting her to the governor's mansion, actually proved that Black candidates could be viable.

CHANG: What about the role of redistricting? Because earlier this year, the Supreme Court struck down a key provision of the Voting Rights Act, right? And many Democrats and voting rights activists thought this would weaken Black voting power. Then we saw a number of Southern states move to redraw congressional maps in a way that experts said would further diminish Black representation across all levels of government. But it doesn't look like that happened. Why not, you think?

GILLESPIE: What we saw across the South in North Carolina, in Tennessee, Texas, you see these instances of Republican voting strength being diluted to try to create as many seats as possible. And what it did in a wave or tsunami election year was create these districts that Democrats could actually compete in.

CHANG: Was there anything about this year's elections that gave you any indications about where the Black vote might go going forward after this particular midterm election?

GILLESPIE: Republicans miscalculated in 2024 that those defections towards the Republican Party in that election were evidence of some type of permanent realignment...

GILLESPIE: ...Instead of looking at what factors might have been influencing people to vote. What that means going forward is that neither party should consider this current election as indicative of what's going to happen in future elections.

CHANG: Andra Gillespie, political science professor at Emory University, thank you very much for joining us today.

GILLESPIE: Thank you. Transcript provided by NPR, Copyright NPR.
